Module 4: Storing & Organizing Collections
4.1 Strings in Depth

Collections

Welcome to Module 4! 🎒

Until now, each of our variables held just a single piece of data (like score = 100 or speed = 45.5).

In this module, you will learn about Collections. A collection is a container that lets you store and organize multiple pieces of data together under one name!

You actually already know the most famous collection in Python: the String! A string is an ordered collection of characters (letters, numbers, spaces, and emojis) all linked together like cars on a train.

Click Next Lesson to inspect strings under a microscope!

Python Strings

In Python, a string is an ordered sequence of characters wrapped in quotation marks.

Every single letter, number, punctuation mark, and space has its own specific spot in line:

Output

The len() function counts every single character in the collection—including blank spaces!

Creating Strings

Python gives you three ways to create strings:

Double Quotes (" "): phrase = "Space Station"

Single Quotes (' '): phrase = 'Space Station'

Triple Quotes (""" """ or ''' '''): Perfect for multiline dialogues, poems, or ASCII art!

Output

Concatenate Strings (Join)

To glue two or more strings together into one long sentence, use the + operator:

Output

(Remember: Python does not add a space automatically with +. You must add " " yourself if you want a space between words!)

Escape Sequences

What happens if you want quotation marks inside your text sentence?

If you type print("He said "Hello!" to me"), Python gets confused by the extra quotes. To fix this, use an escape sequence with a backslash \:

\": Prints a literal double quote without confusing Python.

\': Prints a literal single quote / apostrophe.

\n: Pushes the following text to a brand-new line.

\t: Inserts a tab (4 spaces).

Output

Quiz: Escape Sequences

What will be displayed on the screen by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: Gold\nSilver |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! \n is an escape sequence that Python interprets as an Enter key action. |

| B: Gold Silver on one line |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! \n creates a line break, not a space. |

| C: Gold and Silver on separate lines |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 \n inserts a newline, placing Gold on the first line and Silver on the next. |

| D: A SyntaxError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! \n is completely valid Python syntax. |

Problem Description

Access Characters of a String

Because a string is an ordered collection, every character has an address number called an index:

Plaintext

String:   P  Y  T  H  O  N

Index:    0  1  2  3  4  5

Neg:     -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1

Zero-Based Indexing: The first character is always at index [0].

Negative Indexing: Index [-1] gives the very last character, [-2] gives the second-last, and so on!

Output

Watch Out For IndexError:

If you try to read game[50], Python will throw an IndexError: string index out of range because there is no 50th character!

Quiz: Index Lookup

What is the output of the following code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: R followed by t |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Remember that indexing starts at 0, so vehicle[0] is "R", not vehicle[1]. |

| B: o followed by t |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Index 1 is the second letter ("o"), and index -1 is the last letter ("t"). |

| C: o followed by e |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! [-1] is the very last character, which is "t". |

| D: Rocket |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Square brackets access individual characters, not the full string. |

Strings in Python are IMMUTABLE (unchangeable)! Once created, you cannot swap out individual letters directly.

What if you want to grab an entire chunk of a string (like the first 3 letters)?

You use Slicing:

start is included.

stop is excluded (stops one index before!).

Convenient Shortcuts:

Quiz: Slicing Slices

What is the output of the following slice?

Tap an option below to answer:

String Methods

Python strings come equipped with awesome built-in superpower tools called methods:

.upper(): Converts all letters to uppercase: "cat".upper()  "CAT"

.lower(): Converts all letters to lowercase: "DOG".lower()  "dog"

.replace(old, new): Swaps words: "red car".replace("red", "blue")  "blue car"

.find(sub): Returns the index position of where a word starts: "Galaxy".find("lax")  2

Output

Quiz: The .replace() Method

What will be displayed by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| C: Luigi |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Only the matching word is replaced; the rest of the string remains unchanged. |

| D: An error occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! .replace() is a standard string method. |

4.2 Lists

Introduction to Lists

Imagine you are playing an adventure game. Your character collects a sword, a shield, two health potions, and a map.

If you had to create a separate variable for each item (item1 = "Sword", item2 = "Shield", item3 = "Potion"...), your code would become huge, messy, and hard to manage!

In Python, we solve this using a List.

A list is like a magic adventurer's backpack. It allows you to store, organize, and carry dozens of items inside a single variable!

Click Next Lesson to see how to pack your first list!

Creating Lists

You create a list by placing items inside square brackets [ ] and separating each item with a comma ,:

Output

Cool List Powers:

A list can hold any number of items.

A list can hold mixed data types (str, int, float, bool).

A list can hold duplicate items ([5, 5, 10, 5]).

List Length

To find out how many items are packed inside a list, pass the list into the len() function:

Output

Quiz: Counting List Elements

What is the output of the following code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 3 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Lists allow duplicate items, so "Bravery" is counted each time it appears. |

| B: 4 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 There are 4 total elements packed inside the brackets. len() counts every single item. |

| C: 5 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Count the items separated by commas: there are exactly 4 items. |

| D: None |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! len() returns an integer representing the size of the list. |

Access List Items

Lists are ordered, meaning every item sits in a numbered slot called an index.

Just like strings, list indexing starts at 0:

Plaintext

Negative Indexing

What if you have a massive list of 1,000 items and want to grab the very last item? You don't have to count all the way to 999!

Python supports negative indexing from the back:

[-1]: The very last item!

[-2]: The second-to-last item.

[-3]: The third-to-last item.

Output

Quiz: Negative Index Challenge

Tap an option below to answer:

| Incorrect, give it another shot! colors[-1] is "Yellow", and colors[-2] is "Blue". |

| B: Green |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Counting backwards: -1 is "Yellow", -2 is "Blue", and -3 is "Green"! |

| C: Red |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! "Red" is the first item, which is [-4]. |

| D: An error occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Python fully supports negative indexing. |

Slicing of a List

To extract a smaller sublist from a bigger list, we use slicing:

start is included.

stop is excluded (stops one slot before!).

Click Next Lesson to see slicing in action!

Quiz: Slicing Slices

| Incorrect, give it another shot! The stop index 3 (40) is excluded from the slice. |

| B: [10, 20, 30] |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Index 0 is 10, index 1 is 20, and index 2 is 30 (stops before 3). |

| C: [20, 30, 40] |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! The slice starts at index 0, not 1. |

| D: [10, 20] |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Index 2 (30) is included. |

Omit Start and End Index

You can leave out either the start or stop index for handy shortcuts:

Omit start ([:3]): Slices from the very beginning up to index 2:

Omit stop ([2:]): Slices from index 2 all the way to the end:

Omit both ([:]): Makes a complete copy of the whole list!

4.3 Tuples

Introduction to Tuples

In the previous lesson, you learned about Lists—flexible backpacks where you can add, change, and remove items whenever you want.

Now, imagine you are storing something permanent that should never be changed accidentally:

The GPS coordinates of a secret island: (12.97, 77.59)

The three primary colors: ("Red", "Green", "Blue")

The screen resolution of a game monitor: (1920, 1080)

For permanent data, Python gives us Tuples!

A tuple is an ordered collection of items, just like a list. But there is one big difference: Tuples are IMMUTABLE (unchangeable). Once created, its items are locked in stone forever!

Click Next Lesson to see how to create a tuple!

Creating Tuples

To create a tuple, place items inside round parentheses ( ) separated by commas:

Output

The One-Item Tuple Secret:

If you write item = ("Gold"), Python thinks it's just a regular string! To create a tuple with only one item, you must add a trailing comma:

single_item = ("Gold",) # Now Python knows it's a tuple!

Tuple Length

Just like lists and strings, you can find out how many items are locked inside a tuple using the built-in len() function:

Output

Access Tuple Items

Because tuples are ordered, each item sits at a numbered index, starting at 0:

Plaintext

Tuple:   ("Mercury", "Venus", "Earth")

Index:       [0]       [1]      [2]

Neg:        [-3]      [-2]     [-1]

To fetch an item, put its index inside square brackets [ ]:

Output

Quiz: Tuple Indexing

What will be displayed by this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 13 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Remember that indexing starts at 0 ([0] is 7, [1] is 13). |

| B: 21 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Index 0 is 7, index 1 is 13, and index 2 is 21! |

| C: 42 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! 42 is at index 3. |

| D: A TypeError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Accessing tuple items using [] is completely valid. |

| D: ('B', 'C', 'D') |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Index 1 is 'B', but the slice starts at 2. |

Delete Items of Tuple

In large games or scientific software, tuples act as safety vaults. If another programmer accidentally tries to change game rules or coordinates, Python stops them with an error!

blocks.content: 4.4 Python Sets
Python Sets
Imagine you collect superhero stickers. If your friend gives you a sticker you already have, you don’t need two identical stickers in your album—you only care about having one unique copy of each!
In Python, this is exactly what a Set does!
A Set is a special collection with two superpowers:
No Duplicates Allowed: A set automatically throws away any duplicate items. Every item inside is guaranteed to be 100% unique!
Unordered: Items don’t sit in numbered index slots like lists or tuples. They float inside the collection like marbles in a bag.
Click Next Lesson to create your first set!
Creating Sets
You create a set by placing items inside curly braces { } separated by commas:
Output
Notice that the repeated 2s and 3s were instantly erased! Also, the order might look scrambled on your screen because sets are unordered.
The Empty Set Trap:
Writing {} creates an empty Dictionary, not a set! To create an empty set, you must use the set() function:
empty_chest = set() # The correct way to make an empty set!
Quiz: Duplicate Eraser
How many items will be in this set when it is created?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 5 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Sets never store duplicate items. |

| B: 3 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 The unique items are "Ruby", "Diamond", and "Emerald". All repeated copies are automatically removed, leaving exactly 3 items! |

| C: 2 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! There are three different gem names in the collection. |

| D: A TypeError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Writing duplicate values in a set is valid—Python just cleans them up for you. |
Add and Update Sets
Because sets do not have index slots like [0], you cannot use indexing to change items. Instead, Python gives us two methods:
.add(item): Adds a single new item.
.update(collection): Adds multiple items at once from a list or another set!
Output
Notice that "Knight" was not added a second time because sets keep everything unique!
Practice: Building a Rare Mineral Collection
Problem Description:
Create an empty set named minerals using set().
Add "Quartz" using .add().
Add "Amethyst" using .add().
Try adding "Quartz" again (to see duplicate handling).
Print the minerals set.
Example:
Check if an Item Exists (in and not in)
Sets are lightning-fast at searching! You can check if an item exists inside a set using in:
Output
Quiz: Fast Membership Check
What will be displayed by this code?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: Hero can teleport! |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! "Teleport" is not in the abilities set, so the if condition evaluates to False. |

| B: Ability locked. |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Because "Teleport" is not inside the set, Python runs the else block! |

| C: Both messages |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Only one branch of an if-else statement can run. |

| D: A KeyError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Using in on a set safely returns False without causing an error. |
Set Operators: Union (|)
What if two players want to combine their card collections into one big master deck?
You use the Union operator (|)!
The Union combines all items from both sets, automatically discarding any shared duplicates:
Plaintext
Set A: {"Dog", "Cat"}
Set B: {"Cat", "Parrot"}
Union: {"Dog", "Cat", "Parrot"}
Output
"Leo" was on both teams, but appears only once in the union!
Sets Intersection (&)
What if you want to find the items that two friends have in common?
You use the Intersection operator (&)!
The Intersection returns a new set containing ONLY the items that appear in BOTH sets:
Figure: Two overlapping circles - the shared middle section is the intersection
Output
Delete Items from Sets (.discard())
To remove an item from a set, use the .discard() method:
Output
Why .discard() is Awesome:
If the item doesn't exist, .discard() safely does nothing without crashing your program!

blocks.content: 4.5 Dictionaries
Python Dictionaries
In lists and tuples, you look up items using index numbers like 0, 1, or 2.
But what if you want to look up an item by its name instead of a number?
In a real dictionary, you look up a Word to find its Definition.
In a contact list, you look up a Friend's Name to find their Phone Number.
In a video game, you look up a Stat Name (like "Speed") to find its Value (like 85).
For this, Python gives us one of its most powerful collections: the Dictionary!
A dictionary stores information in Key-Value Pairs:
Key: The unique label you search for (e.g., "Health").
Value: The data attached to that label (e.g., 100).

4.6 Data Structure Conversions
Python Conversion
You’ve now met the four main collection types in Python:
Lists ([ ]): Changeable and ordered.
Tuples (( )): Locked and unchangeable.
Sets ({ }): Unordered and duplicate-free.
Dictionaries ({k: v}): Labeled key-value lookups.
Sometimes you start with one collection type, but need to shape-shift it into another:
You have a locked tuple, but you need to add an item to it  Convert to a list!
You have a list full of messy duplicate entries  Convert to a set to clean them!
Python provides four built-in conversion functions: list(), tuple(), set(), and dict().
Click Next Lesson to start converting!
